questions.q: What is the numbered, sequential migration script pattern?
options: Every schema change is its own small, self-contained script, numbered in the order it must run
One giant script containing the entire schema's history in a single file
Migrations are applied in a random order determined at runtime
Each developer maintains a private, unnumbered set of migration scripts
questions.explain: Numbering each self-contained migration script guarantees a consistent, predictable application order across every environment.

questions.q: What does a migrations-tracking table actually do?
options: Records, in the target database, which migration numbers have already been applied there
Stores a full backup copy of every table before a migration runs
Tracks the names of developers who wrote each migration, nothing else
Automatically rewrites old migrations to match new coding standards
questions.explain: The tracking table is what lets a migration runner know which migrations are already applied versus which still need to run.

questions.q: Why is it safe to rerun the same migration pipeline step against a database that's already fully up to date?
options: The runner checks the tracking table and finds every migration already recorded, so nothing runs
SQL Server automatically skips any pipeline step run more than once
The pipeline deletes the database and rebuilds it from scratch every single run
It isn't safe — rerunning against an up-to-date database always causes errors
questions.explain: Because the tracking table records what's already applied, a rerun against an up-to-date database is a no-op.

questions.q: Why are migrations additive — why not just edit an already-applied migration script to fix a mistake in it?
options: Anyone who already ran the old version has a database that no longer matches, and the tracking table would wrongly say it's already applied
Git technically prevents editing any file that has been committed once
SQL Server caches migration scripts and ignores any edits automatically
There's no real reason; editing an old migration is equally acceptable
questions.explain: Once a migration has run against real environments, it's already a fact on disk elsewhere — editing it retroactively creates inconsistency.

questions.q: What is the correct way to fix a mistake in an already-deployed migration, per this lesson?
options: Write a new migration that corrects the problem going forward
Directly edit the old migration file and redeploy it everywhere
Delete the migrations-tracking table and start over
Manually fix the mistake by hand on every environment with no script at all
questions.explain: A new, later-numbered migration is the additive, safe way to correct a previously deployed mistake.
